subject: history
topicDisplay: Power and the People, c1170 to present day
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Who was the Archbishop of Canterbury murdered in Canterbury Cathedral in 1170?
questions.explain: Thomas Becket was murdered in 1170 after his long conflict with Henry II over the power of the Church versus the Crown.

questions.q: In which year was Magna Carta sealed by King John at Runnymede?
questions.explain: King John was forced by rebellious barons to seal Magna Carta at Runnymede in 1215, limiting royal power.

questions.q: What made Simon de Montfort's parliament of 1265 significant?
options: It was the first parliament to include elected burgesses from towns as well as knights
It gave women the right to vote
It ended the feudal system entirely
questions.explain: De Montfort's 1265 parliament was the first to summon burgesses from the towns, widening representation beyond the nobility.

questions.q: Who was the main leader of the Peasants' Revolt of 1381?
questions.explain: Wat Tyler led the rebels to London and was killed at Smithfield by the Lord Mayor, William Walworth.

questions.q: Which grievance was the main trigger of the Peasants' Revolt in 1381?
questions.explain: A series of unpopular Poll Taxes to fund war with France was the immediate spark for the 1381 revolt.

questions.q: The preacher John Ball asked, 'When Adam delved and Eve span, who was then the gentleman?' This appeal to social equality was linked to which event?
questions.explain: John Ball's radical preaching about natural equality helped inspire the peasants who rose up in 1381.

questions.q: The Pilgrimage of Grace (1536) was a rebellion against which of Henry VIII's policies?
options: The introduction of the Poll Tax
The abolition of the slave trade
questions.explain: The Pilgrimage of Grace was a mainly northern protest against religious changes, especially the closure of the monasteries.

questions.q: Who was the leader of the Pilgrimage of Grace in 1536?
questions.explain: The Yorkshire lawyer Robert Aske led the Pilgrimage of Grace and was later executed for his part in it.

questions.q: Which of the following was a major cause of conflict between Charles I and Parliament?
options: His collection of taxes such as Ship Money without Parliament's consent
His support for extending the vote to women
questions.explain: Charles I's belief in the Divine Right of Kings and taxes like Ship Money raised without Parliament helped cause the Civil War.

questions.q: In which year was King Charles I executed?
questions.explain: After defeat in the Civil War, Charles I was tried and executed in January 1649, leading to a republic.

questions.q: What did the Levellers, led by figures such as John Lilburne, campaign for during the English Revolution?
options: A wider extension of the right to vote and a written constitution
The restoration of the monarchy's absolute power
questions.explain: The Levellers argued in documents like the Agreement of the People for wider suffrage and greater political rights.

questions.q: The slogan 'No taxation without representation' came from which event that later inspired British reformers?
questions.explain: American colonists' demand for representation before taxation influenced later British campaigns for the vote.

questions.q: In which year was the Great Reform Act passed?
questions.explain: The Great Reform Act of 1832 was the first major reform of Parliament, though it still left most men without the vote.

questions.q: What was one important effect of the 1832 Reform Act?
options: It removed many rotten boroughs and gave seats to growing industrial towns
It gave all adults the right to vote
It gave women over 30 the vote
It abolished the House of Lords
questions.explain: The 1832 Act redistributed seats away from rotten boroughs to expanding industrial towns such as Manchester and Birmingham.

questions.q: A campaigner in 1839 demands a secret ballot and payment for MPs so that working men can stand for Parliament. Which movement do they belong to?
questions.explain: The secret ballot and payment of MPs were among the six points of the People's Charter demanded by the Chartists.

questions.q: The Tolpuddle Martyrs were transported to Australia in 1834 for forming what?
questions.explain: The Dorset farm labourers were transported for swearing a secret oath while setting up a trade union to protest low wages.

questions.q: Why were the Tolpuddle Martyrs significant for the trade union movement?
options: The public outcry at their harsh punishment built support for trade unionism and led to their pardon
They won the vote for all working men
questions.explain: Mass protests against their transportation became a rallying point for early trade unions, and the men were eventually pardoned.

questions.q: Who founded the Women's Social and Political Union (WSPU) in 1903?
questions.explain: Emmeline Pankhurst founded the militant WSPU in 1903 under the slogan 'Deeds not words'.

questions.q: What was the main difference between the suffragists (NUWSS) and the suffragettes (WSPU)?
options: The suffragists used peaceful, lawful methods while the suffragettes used militant direct action
The suffragists wanted votes for men only
The suffragettes opposed votes for women
There was no real difference between them
questions.explain: The NUWSS suffragists campaigned peacefully, whereas the WSPU suffragettes used militant tactics such as protests and hunger strikes.

questions.q: In 1963 campaigners led by Paul Stephenson organised a boycott after a company refused to employ Black or Asian bus crews. Which event was this?
questions.explain: The 1963 Bristol Bus Boycott successfully challenged a colour bar and helped pave the way for the Race Relations Acts.
